aeo.what_is: Intrusive unwanted thoughts driving repetitive behaviors to reduce anxiety or prevent feared outcomes.

description.overview: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both. Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are intrusive and unwanted, causing marked anxiety or distress. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules. These behaviors aim to reduce distress or prevent a feared event, but are excessive or not realistically connected to the event. The obsessions or compulsions cause significant distress, are time-consuming, or interfere with daily functioning.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A parent who repeatedly checks that the stove is off, even after confirming it multiple times, fearing the house will burn down.
A college student who arranges books and belongings in perfect symmetry, restarting if anything feels 'off' or uneven.
A professional who spends hours washing and rewashing hands until they feel 'clean enough,' despite skin irritation.
A teenager who counts to specific numbers mentally before performing everyday actions to prevent bad things from happening.
A driver who circles back repeatedly to check they didn't hit someone, despite no evidence of impact.
A person who avoids touching doorknobs or public surfaces due to overwhelming contamination fears.
Someone who experiences intrusive violent images and prays repeatedly to neutralize the thoughts.
A worker who checks and rechecks emails dozens of times before sending, fearing they made a mistake.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief at finally having an explanation for confusing and distressing symptoms.
Shame or embarrassment about the nature of intrusive thoughts, especially taboo ones.
Hope that treatment can reduce the exhausting cycle of obsessions and compulsions.
Fear that others will judge them as 'crazy' or dangerous if they share their thoughts.
Confusion about why they can't just 'stop' the rituals even when they recognize they're excessive.
Anxiety about exposure therapy and facing feared situations without compulsions.
Validation that their experience is recognized and treatable, not a character flaw.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both. B. Obsessions and/or compulsions are time-consuming (e.g., >1 hour/day) or cause clinically significant distress/impairment. C. Symptoms are not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition. D. Disturbance is not better explained by another mental disorder.

temporal_criteria.duration: Obsessions and/or compulsions must be time-consuming (typically taking more than 1 hour per day) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
temporal_criteria.course_pattern: Often chronic and waxing/waning; symptoms may worsen during stress and improve with treatment.
temporal_criteria.onset_timeline: Bimodal onset with peaks in childhood/adolescence and early adulthood; can emerge gradually or suddenly.
temporal_criteria.acute_vs_chronic: Usually chronic without treatment; acute exacerbations can occur during life stressors or transitions.

content.prevalence: 12-month prevalence about 1.2% in the U.S.; similar rates in males and females, though males have earlier onset.
content.age_of_onset: Bimodal onset — one peak in childhood/adolescence and another in early adulthood.
content.prognosis: Often chronic without treatment; early intervention improves outcomes. Many have waxing and waning symptoms. Good insight, lower baseline severity, and strong support are associated with better prognosis.

circuitry: Hyperactivity in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loops, especially orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and caudate nucleus.
neurochemistry: Serotonergic system dysfunction; possible glutamate dysregulation.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: First-degree relatives have increased risk; early-life stress, infection (PANDAS/PANS hypotheses) may contribute.

history_psychosocial: Specific obsessions and compulsions, avoidance behaviors.
Impact on school/work/home, relationships, and leisure.
medical_assessment: Assess for tics or neurological findings if relevant.
Screen for autoimmune or infectious triggers in suspected pediatric-onset (PANDAS/PANS).
risk_stratification: Assess for suicidal ideation due to comorbid depression or distress from symptoms.
evaluation.team_and_process: Interdisciplinary care with psychiatry, psychology, and when indicated neurology or pediatrics; involve family in psychoeducation and support.

obsessions: Fears of harming self or others

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms cause some distress but minimal interference with functioning.
severity_levels.moderate: Symptoms cause clear distress and interfere with functioning, but manageable with effort.
severity_levels.severe: Symptoms are disabling and prevent normal functioning.

biological: Family history of OCD or related disorders

impact_on_life.school_work: Reduced productivity, absenteeism due to rituals or avoidance.
impact_on_life.medical: Skin damage from excessive washing, musculoskeletal pain from repetitive actions.

psychotherapy: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) — gold standard behavioral treatment.
Cognitive therapy targeting maladaptive beliefs about responsibility and threat.
medications: First-line: SSRIs (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram).
Clomipramine — effective but with more side effects; monitor for cardiac and anticholinergic effects.
Augmentation: low-dose antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) for partial SSRI responders.
neuromodulation: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) for severe, treatment-refractory cases.
Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) targeting supplementary motor area.
lifestyle_interventions: Stress management, mindfulness, regular sleep and exercise.
care_coordination: Close monitoring of medication adherence and ERP participation.
Involving support network for encouragement and assistance.

treatment_goals: Reduce severity and frequency of obsessions and compulsions.
Improve functional ability and quality of life.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Misattributing intrusive thoughts to psychosis without assessing insight.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling normative routines or preferences as compulsions.

often_confused_with.why: Both involve excessive worry, but GAD worries are about real-life concerns while OCD obsessions are intrusive, unwanted, and often irrational.
often_confused_with.key_difference: OCD has specific compulsions or mental rituals performed to reduce anxiety; GAD does not.

often_confused_with.why: Intrusive violent or bizarre thoughts in OCD can be mistaken for delusions or hallucinations.
often_confused_with.key_difference: People with OCD recognize thoughts as their own and as excessive (good insight); psychotic individuals lack this insight.

often_confused_with.why: Both can involve repetitive behaviors and need for sameness/routines.
often_confused_with.key_difference: OCD behaviors are driven by anxiety and distress; autism routines provide comfort and aren't anxiety-driven compulsions.

often_confused_with.why: Both involve obsessive preoccupations and repetitive behaviors (checking, grooming).
often_confused_with.key_difference: BDD obsessions are specifically about perceived appearance flaws; OCD themes are broader and more varied.

red_flags_for_misdiagnosis: Labeling normal preferences for order or cleanliness as OCD without assessing distress or impairment.
Missing covert mental compulsions (counting, praying, reviewing) and only looking for visible rituals.
Assuming harm-related intrusive thoughts mean the person is dangerous or psychotic.
Not distinguishing between ego-syntonic habits and ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions.

insight: Good/fair insight: recognizes OCD beliefs are probably not true
Poor insight: thinks OCD beliefs are probably true
tic_related: Current or past history of tic disorder

warning_signs: Escalating distress and impairment from rituals
Skin lesions, infections from excessive cleaning
self_help_strategies: Gradual exposure to feared situations without rituals.
Self-monitoring of triggers and compulsive urges.

childhood: Magical thinking and rituals; possible comorbid tics.
adolescence: Increased time spent on rituals; school and social impairment.
adulthood: Chronic symptoms; occupational and relationship strain.

first_person_statements: I know logically that I locked the door, but the doubt feels so real that I have to go back and check again and again until it feels 'right.'
The intrusive thoughts are terrifying and completely against who I am, but they won't stop coming no matter how hard I try to push them away.
Washing my hands gives me a few seconds of relief, but then the contamination fear comes rushing back and I have to start all over again.
People think I'm just being neat or particular, but they don't understand the panic I feel if things aren't perfectly symmetrical.
I spend hours every day on rituals I know don't make sense, but I'm too afraid of what might happen if I don't do them.
The worst part isn't the rituals themselves, it's the shame of knowing how irrational it all is but feeling powerless to stop.

real_life_examples.presentation: Maria, a 32-year-old mother, spends over two hours every night checking locks, appliances, and windows before bed. Even after checking the stove multiple times and confirming it's off, she's gripped by the fear that she missed something and her family will die in a fire. She sets alarms to wake up and recheck during the night. Her husband has started sleeping in another room because her constant getting up disturbs his sleep. Maria knows rationally that the stove is off, but the doubt feels unbearable and she can't resist the urge to check 'just one more time.'
real_life_examples.daily_impact: Sleep deprivation, marital strain, exhaustion affecting her ability to care for her children, growing shame about her inability to stop despite knowing it's excessive.

real_life_examples.presentation: David, a 19-year-old college student, washes his hands 50-60 times a day until they're cracked and bleeding. He avoids touching doorknobs, sitting on public chairs, or shaking hands. In his dorm, he has elaborate cleaning rituals that take up to three hours daily. He wears gloves constantly and uses paper towels to touch everything. If he accidentally touches something he deems contaminated, he must shower immediately and wash all his clothes. He's dropped classes because he couldn't tolerate the 'contaminated' environment.
real_life_examples.daily_impact: Academic failure, social isolation, severe skin damage requiring medical treatment, inability to participate in normal college activities, spending most of his day consumed by cleaning rituals.

real_life_examples.presentation: James, a 28-year-old accountant, is plagued by intrusive violent images of harming others, particularly stabbing. These thoughts terrify him because they're completely against his values. He avoids kitchens and hides all sharp objects. He prays and mentally reviews his character for hours to 'prove' he's not violent. He's too ashamed to tell anyone about these thoughts and secretly fears he might be a dangerous person. He's started avoiding his nieces and nephews because the thoughts are worse around children.
real_life_examples.daily_impact: Constant distress and self-doubt, avoidance of family gatherings, hours spent on mental rituals, growing isolation, and fear that he's losing his mind or is secretly evil.

real_life_examples.presentation: Aisha, a 16-year-old high school student, needs everything to feel 'even' or 'balanced.' She touches objects multiple times until it feels right, aligns items perfectly, and repeats actions an even number of times. If she steps on a crack with her left foot, she must step on one with her right foot. Getting ready for school takes three hours because she redoes makeup, hair, and outfit choices until they feel symmetrical. She's chronically late and her grades are slipping because she spends class time arranging her desk and supplies instead of listening.
real_life_examples.daily_impact: Academic decline, chronic lateness, exhaustion, frustration from parents who don't understand why she can't 'just hurry up,' and increasing anxiety as rituals expand to more areas of her life.

real_life_examples.presentation: Robert, a 45-year-old sales manager, drives the same route repeatedly after hitting even minor bumps, convinced he's struck a pedestrian. He circles back 10-15 times per trip, checking for bodies or evidence of impact. He scours news reports for hit-and-run accidents in areas he's driven. A 20-minute commute now takes two hours. He's been late to important meetings and his job performance is suffering. He's considered giving up driving entirely but needs his car for work.
real_life_examples.daily_impact: Job jeopardy, excessive time spent driving and checking, high anxiety during all car trips, relationship strain as family members refuse to drive with him, and growing despair about his inability to stop despite no evidence of ever hitting anyone.

similarities: Both involve excessive worry and anxiety
Both can cause significant distress and functional impairment
Both may respond to SSRIs and CBT
differences: OCD: Specific intrusive obsessions and compulsive rituals; GAD: Broad, diffuse worry about life circumstances
OCD: Compulsions temporarily reduce anxiety; GAD: No ritualistic behaviors tied to worries
OCD: Thoughts feel intrusive and ego-dystonic; GAD: Worries feel like excessive but understandable responses to real concerns
OCD: Responds best to ERP; GAD: Responds to general CBT without need for exposure hierarchy

similarities: Both involve intense fear or anxiety about specific objects or situations
Both can lead to avoidance behaviors
differences: OCD: Fear triggers elaborate compulsions or mental rituals; Phobia: Fear triggers simple avoidance
OCD: Multiple obsessional themes often present; Phobia: Usually circumscribed to one trigger
OCD: Time-consuming rituals central to disorder; Phobia: No ritualistic behaviors, just avoidance
OCD: Often poor insight about excessiveness; Phobia: Usually recognizes fear is excessive

similarities: Both involve obsessive preoccupations causing significant distress
Both can severely impact functioning and quality of life
Both respond to SSRIs and may benefit from ERP
differences: OCD: Diverse obsession themes; BDD: Exclusively focused on perceived appearance flaws
OCD: Compulsions aim to prevent harm or reduce general anxiety; BDD: Behaviors specifically target appearance concerns
OCD: Insight varies; BDD: Often very poor insight about actual appearance
OCD: May have no appearance concerns; BDD: Appearance is central focus

similarities: Both may involve perfectionism and rigidity
Both can include preoccupation with orderliness and control
Both can impact relationships and work
differences: OCD: Ego-dystonic (unwanted, distressing); OCPD: Ego-syntonic (viewed as correct way to be)
OCD: Specific obsessions and compulsions; OCPD: Pervasive personality pattern without true obsessions/compulsions
OCD: Causes marked distress; OCPD: Often distresses others more than the individual
OCD: Responds to ERP and SSRIs; OCPD: Requires longer-term personality-focused therapy

faqs.question: Does everyone with OCD wash their hands excessively?
faqs.answer: No, contamination fears and washing are just one type of OCD. Many people have obsessions about harm, symmetry, intrusive taboo thoughts, or other themes without any contamination concerns.

faqs.question: If I like things neat and organized, do I have OCD?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. OCD involves distressing, intrusive obsessions and time-consuming compulsions that interfere with your life. Preferring organization without distress or impairment is just a personality trait, not a disorder.

faqs.question: Are intrusive violent or sexual thoughts in OCD dangerous?
faqs.answer: No. These thoughts are ego-dystonic (unwanted and distressing), completely opposite to the person's values, and people with OCD are not more likely to act on them. The thoughts cause anxiety precisely because they're so contrary to who the person is.

faqs.question: Can I just use willpower to stop my compulsions?
faqs.answer: OCD isn't a matter of willpower or self-control. It's a neurobiological disorder involving specific brain circuits. Effective treatment (especially ERP) teaches you how to tolerate anxiety without compulsions, but this requires structured therapeutic support, not just willpower.

faqs.question: Will medication cure my OCD?
faqs.answer: Medication, particularly SSRIs or clomipramine, can significantly reduce OCD symptoms, but it's not typically a cure. Combining medication with ERP therapy provides the best outcomes, and many people need ongoing treatment to maintain improvement.

faqs.question: What is ERP and why is it so important for OCD?
faqs.answer: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is a therapy where you gradually face feared situations (exposure) while resisting the urge to perform compulsions (response prevention). It's the gold standard treatment because it directly breaks the OCD cycle and retrains your brain's response to obsessions.

faqs.question: How long does OCD treatment take?
faqs.answer: ERP typically involves 12-20 sessions for noticeable improvement, though severe OCD may require longer treatment. Medication effects emerge in 8-12 weeks. Many people continue maintenance treatment long-term to prevent relapse.

faqs.question: Can OCD go away on its own?
faqs.answer: OCD rarely resolves without treatment and is typically chronic. While symptoms may wax and wane, they usually persist and can worsen over time without intervention. Early treatment significantly improves long-term outcomes.

faqs.question: Is OCD the same as being a perfectionist?
faqs.answer: No. Perfectionism is a personality trait where someone sets high standards and strives to meet them. OCD involves intrusive, unwanted obsessions causing severe anxiety, with compulsions performed to reduce that anxiety, often unrelated to achieving excellence.

faqs.question: Can children have OCD?
faqs.answer: Yes, OCD often begins in childhood or adolescence. Children may have typical OCD symptoms or presentations like PANDAS/PANS (sudden onset after infection). Treatment includes family-based ERP and sometimes medication.

faqs.question: Why do my OCD symptoms change over time?
faqs.answer: It's common for obsession themes and compulsions to shift. Your brain may find new triggers or develop new patterns. This doesn't mean treatment failed; it means continuing or adjusting ERP to target new symptoms.

faqs.question: Should I tell my family about my intrusive thoughts?
faqs.answer: Sharing with trusted people can reduce shame and isolation, but only when you're ready and with people who will be supportive. A therapist can help you decide how and when to disclose, and what information is helpful to share.

faqs.question: Can stress make OCD worse?
faqs.answer: Yes, stress commonly exacerbates OCD symptoms. Major life changes, trauma, or ongoing stress can increase obsession frequency and compulsion intensity. Stress management is an important part of comprehensive OCD treatment.

faqs.question: What if ERP makes my anxiety too overwhelming?
faqs.answer: ERP is conducted gradually, starting with lower-anxiety exposures and building up. A skilled therapist will work at a pace that's challenging but tolerable. If anxiety becomes too intense, exposures can be adjusted. The goal is manageable discomfort, not overwhelming distress.

faqs.question: Is OCD genetic?
faqs.answer: OCD has a genetic component; first-degree relatives have higher risk. However, genetics aren't destiny; environmental factors also play a role. Having a family history increases risk but doesn't guarantee you'll develop OCD.

faqs.question: Can I drink alcohol if I'm taking medication for OCD?
faqs.answer: Alcohol can interact with OCD medications, particularly increasing sedation or side effects. It can also worsen OCD symptoms and interfere with treatment progress. Discuss any alcohol use with your prescriber.

faqs.question: Why do I need to do compulsions so many times before it feels 'right'?
faqs.answer: OCD affects your brain's ability to register completion of tasks and tolerate uncertainty. The 'not just right' feeling is a symptom of OCD, not a reliable signal. ERP helps retrain your brain to tolerate that feeling without acting on it.

faqs.question: What's the difference between obsessions and compulsions?
faqs.answer: Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges causing anxiety. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce that anxiety or prevent feared outcomes. Most people with OCD have both, but some have primarily obsessions or primarily compulsions.

faqs.question: Can OCD lead to other mental health problems?
faqs.answer: Yes, untreated OCD commonly co-occurs with depression, other anxiety disorders, eating disorders, or tic disorders. The chronic stress and impairment from OCD can contribute to developing these conditions. Treating OCD can help prevent or improve comorbid conditions.

faqs.question: Will I ever be completely free of intrusive thoughts?
faqs.answer: Most people, even without OCD, have occasional intrusive thoughts. The goal of treatment isn't to eliminate all intrusive thoughts, but to change your relationship with them so they don't cause distress or drive compulsions. You learn they're just thoughts, not meaningful or dangerous.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek help if obsessions or compulsions take more than an hour a day, cause distress, or impair functioning.

positive_factors: Strong adherence to ERP and medications
